item.title: $41,929 raised for Gospel Schools during Blue Sapphire anniversary celebrations
item.description: A total of $41,929 has been raised during the 65-day Gospel Schools Blue Sapphire Anniversary celebrations, with the funds expected to support the primary and secondary schools, as well as the Gospel School for the Deaf. The money was collected through contributions from different groups of former students who came together to support their former schools.
item.content:encoded:
A total of $41,929 has been raised during the 65-day Gospel Schools Blue Sapphire Anniversary celebrations, with the funds expected to support the primary and secondary schools, as well as the Gospel School for the Deaf.

The money was collected through contributions from different groups of former students who came together to support their former schools.

Newly elected Gospel Ex-Scholars Association Chairperson Alvin Avikash Nair says the incoming committee will first assess the needs of the schools before deciding how the funds will be allocated.

Nair says the committee will work together to ensure the money is used effectively for the benefit of the schools and their students.

He was elected during the association's executive committee elections, alongside three other office-bearers who will lead the association.

The elections involved both online and in-person voting, allowing former students living overseas and those unable to attend in person to participate.

In his first remarks as chairperson, Nair thanked members for placing their confidence in him and expressed his commitment to working with the new committee and fellow candidates.

He also acknowledged the outgoing committee for its efforts in organising the Blue Sapphire Anniversary celebrations.

The celebrations will continue at 6pm this evening at the Darul-Huda Complex on Brown Street, with a kava session and a live Sigidrigi band.

The Blue Dawn Prayer Breakfast will be held at 7am tomorrow at Foster Crane Hall, followed by the Blue Sapphire Jubilee Ball at 6pm at the Vodafone Arena.

The celebrations will conclude with a Thanksgiving Church Service at the school hall at 3pm on Sunday.

item.title: Ba resident calls for urgent Government assistance and long-term drought management strategy
item.description: The prolonged drought conditions associated with El Niño are a serious concern for Ba and the wider Western Division. This has been stressed by Vatulaulau resident Shalen Andrew, who says the impact extends beyond water shortages, affecting livelihoods, food security, agricultural production, businesses, public health and the overall economic wellbeing of communities.
item.content:encoded:
The prolonged drought conditions associated with El Niño are a serious concern for Ba and the wider Western Division.

This has been stressed by Vatulaulau resident Shalen Andrew, who says the impact extends beyond water shortages, affecting livelihoods, food security, agricultural production, businesses, public health and the overall economic wellbeing of communities.

Andrew is calling for immediate Government intervention to prioritise affected communities through emergency water carting, accessible water distribution points and regular monitoring of water supplies.

He is also recommending targeted assistance for farmers through the provision of drought-resistant crops, irrigation equipment, livestock feed and technical advice.

Andrew is calling for greater investment in water tanks, rainwater harvesting systems, sustainable boreholes and improved water infrastructure to strengthen water security in communities.

He says targeted financial assistance should also be considered for vulnerable households, small farmers and businesses experiencing significant drought-related losses.

Andrew is also stressing the importance of ensuring access to safe drinking water, raising awareness about sanitation and regularly monitoring water quality to protect public health.

He says the current situation should serve as an important lesson for Fiji, highlighting the need to move beyond emergency responses and develop a sustainable national drought management strategy.

Andrew says this should include improved water storage, climate-resilient agriculture, early warning systems and dedicated disaster response funding.

He says the impact of prolonged drought can be far-reaching, affecting not only immediate water supplies but also food security, livelihoods, economic activity and the wellbeing of future generations.

Andrew is appealing for timely Government action, practical assistance for affected communities and stronger cooperation between all stakeholders.

He says people should not have to wait until the situation becomes critical before meaningful action is taken.

Andrew stresses that water is a basic necessity, food security is a national priority and protecting communities is a shared responsibility.

He adds that Fiji must be prepared, Ba must be supported and people must come first.

item.title: University of Fiji considers online classes if drought restrictions affect campuses
item.description: The University of Fiji is preparing for the possibility of shifting to online learning and flexible working arrangements if drought-related restrictions affect campus operations. This follows the Ministry of Education's announcement that primary and secondary schools will close due to the National State of Disaster.
item.content:encoded:
The University of Fiji is preparing for the possibility of shifting to online learning and flexible working arrangements if drought-related restrictions affect campus operations.

This follows the Ministry of Education's announcement that primary and secondary schools will close due to the National State of Disaster.

University of Fiji Vice-Chancellor Professor Shaista Shameem says the Ministry's announcement currently applies only to primary and secondary schools and does not include universities.

However, she says the university is preparing for the possibility of similar restrictions being introduced for tertiary institutions.

Professor Shameem says the university has a National Disaster Policy and Plan in place to ensure teaching, learning and essential operations can continue during emergencies.

She says the university can use its TopHat online learning platform to allow students to continue their studies and staff to work remotely if they are unable to attend campus.

The Vice-Chancellor says most students have already completed their examinations and are therefore unlikely to be significantly affected by any changes to campus operations.

However, some staff are still attending meetings and completing their work for the year.

Professor Shameem says deans and department heads have been asked to consider alternative working arrangements if the university needs to operate with only essential staff during the drought.

The university's Disaster Management Committee is also expected to meet this week to assess the potential impact of the current conditions on its operations.

She says the university's disaster plan was initially developed during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since been updated to cover other national emergencies.

Professor Shameem says the university will continue working closely with the Ministry of Education to ensure students can continue learning if dry conditions persist or worsen.

item.title: Founders' sacrifices remembered as Gospel Schools mark 65 years
item.description: Gospel High School was built on blood, sweat and tears, with its founders making personal sacrifices to establish a school where children in Fiji could learn about Jesus. This was shared by long-time educator and mentor Naomi McKinnon during the 65th day of celebrations marking Gospel Schools' Blue Sapphire Anniversary at the school hall at Dhanji Street.
item.content:encoded:
Gospel High School was built on blood, sweat and tears, with its founders making personal sacrifices to establish a school where children in Fiji could learn about Jesus.

This was shared by long-time educator and mentor Naomi McKinnon during the 65th day of celebrations marking Gospel Schools' Blue Sapphire Anniversary at the school hall at Dhanji Street.

McKinnon reflected on the sacrifices made by founder Foster Crane and his wife Gwen, who spent 22 years in Fiji before receiving the vision to establish the school.

She says they founded churches, walked across islands through the mud and struggled before God gave them the vision to build the school.

McKinnon says Foster Crane was not sitting in an office overseeing the construction, but was personally involved as a builder.

She says the primary school was built first, with builders and funding coming from New Zealand, while Arthur Crane, who was about 16 years old at the time, helped by painting the roof.

As the children grew older, the need for a high school emerged, with the institution gradually built in stages as funds became available.

McKinnon says Foster Crane continued building the school in 1967 despite suffering from boils nearly all over his body.

He said it was terrible just to lift a hammer but he did it. He kept doing it. They worked together.

McKinnon also acknowledged the contribution of founding teachers, including Miss Macdonald, who helped establish the high school.

Reflecting on her own journey, McKinnon says she arrived at Gospel High School at the age of 25 in 1970 and taught there until 2005.

She recalls struggling to pronounce students' names on her first day, saying she called out the roll without knowing how to pronounce anybody's name.

McKinnon says her years at the school shaped her as a teacher and taught her to love people, while her students also taught her how to teach.

She says she had to study and understand the language challenges students faced, particularly in mathematics.

One of the challenges was the lack of a Fijian word for similar triangles, prompting her to invent the term 'tautauvata squared'.

McKinnon says Fiji remains in her heart and she takes Fiji everywhere she goes.

She says Gospel Schools is also her school because it is where she learned to be a teacher and developed her love for people.

The anniversary celebrations began today with a march involving students from different decades, starting from BSP Bank along Dhanji Road before proceeding to Gospel High School for the official opening ceremony at Foster Crane Hall.

A market day is also being held on the school grounds, providing an opportunity for the Gospel family to reconnect, fellowship and celebrate together.

The celebrations will continue this evening at 6pm at the Darul-Huda complex at Brown Street with kava and a Sigidrigi live band.

Tomorrow morning at 7am, there will be a Blue Dawn Prayer Breakfast at Foster Crane Hall, and at 6pm, the Blue Sapphire Jubilee Ball at the Vodafone Arena.

The Thanksgiving Church Service will be held at the school hall at 3pm Sunday.
